prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The formation of quasi-2D spin-wave waveforms in longitudinally magnetized stripes of ferrimagnetic film was observed by using time- and space-resolved Brillouin light scattering technique. In the linear regime it was found that the confinement decreases the amplitude of dynamic magnetization near the lateral stripe edges. Thus, the so-called effective dipolar pinning of dynamic magnetization takes place at the edges.   In the nonlinear regime a new stable spin wave packet propagating along a waveguide structure, for which both transversal instability and interaction with the side walls of the waveguide are important was observed. The experiments and a numerical simulation of the pulse evolution show that the shape of the formed waveforms and their behavior are strongly influenced by the confinement.

In the linear regime, lateral confinement was shown to reduce the dynamic magnetization amplitude close to the stripe boundaries. This indicates the presence of effective dipolar pinning of the dynamic magnetization at the edges.

Quasi-two-dimensional spin-wave waveforms were observed in longitudinally magnetized ferrimagnetic film stripes by means of time- and space-resolved Brillouin light scattering. This experimental technique made it possible to directly map the evolution of spin-wave excitations both in time and across the spatial profile of the waveguide.

In the linear excitation regime, the finite lateral size of the stripe was found to have a pronounced effect on the distribution of the dynamic magnetization. In particular, the spin-wave amplitude was reduced near the lateral edges of the stripe. This behavior indicates that the boundaries of the waveguide do not simply act as passive geometrical limits, but significantly modify the spin-wave mode structure.

The observed reduction of the dynamic magnetization at the stripe edges can be attributed to effective dipolar pinning. Due to dipolar interactions, the dynamic magnetization becomes constrained near the lateral boundaries, leading to a nonuniform transverse mode profile. As a result, the spin-wave modes in the confined stripe differ substantially from those in an extended film.

In the nonlinear regime, the experiments revealed the formation of a new stable spin-wave packet propagating along the waveguide structure. This packet maintained its shape during propagation, demonstrating that nonlinear effects, together with dispersion and confinement, can support robust localized waveforms in ferrimagnetic film stripes.

Both experimental observations and numerical simulations confirmed that lateral confinement plays a crucial role in determining the shape, stability, and propagation behavior of the generated spin-wave waveforms. The results show that the geometry of the magnetic waveguide strongly influences the dynamic magnetization profile and the nonlinear spin-wave dynamics, making confinement an essential factor in the design and understanding of spin-wave-based devices.

Time- and space-resolved Brillouin light scattering was employed to investigate the propagation of quasi-two-dimensional spin-wave waveforms in longitudinally magnetized ferrimagnetic film stripes. The work focused on how the finite lateral width of the stripes influences both the linear and nonlinear dynamics of spin waves, with particular attention to the role of confinement imposed by the stripe edges.

In the linear propagation regime, the measurements revealed that the lateral boundaries of the waveguide strongly modify the spin-wave mode structure. The observed behavior is consistent with effective dipolar pinning at the stripe edges, which restricts the transverse spin-wave profile and determines the allowed lateral modes. As a result, the spin waves cannot be treated simply as plane waves propagating in an extended film; instead, their dynamics are governed by the waveguide geometry and by the boundary conditions imposed at the side walls.

In the nonlinear regime, the experiments showed even richer behavior. The interplay between lateral confinement, nonlinear self-action, transversal instability, and reflections or interactions at the stripe side walls leads to the formation of a previously unobserved stable nonlinear spin-wave packet. This packet is not solely determined by the intrinsic nonlinear properties of the ferrimagnetic film, but also by the spatial restrictions imposed by the stripe geometry. The confinement therefore plays an active role in shaping the waveform, stabilizing its structure, and influencing its propagation characteristics.

These results demonstrate that the dynamics of spin waves in magnetic film stripes are strongly controlled by waveguide geometry. Lateral confinement affects the mode spectrum in the linear regime and can give rise to new stable nonlinear excitations when the spin-wave amplitude is increased. The study highlights the importance of boundary conditions, dipolar pinning, and side-wall interactions in confined magnetic systems, and it emphasizes that careful control of waveguide dimensions can be used to tailor spin-wave propagation in magnonic devices.

The Brillouin zone is an important concept in solid-state physics, especially in the study of crystals and their electronic properties. It describes a unique region in reciprocal space that helps scientists understand how waves, such as electron waves, behave inside a periodic lattice.

Brillouin zones are used to analyze the energy levels of electrons in materials. When electrons move through a crystal, their behavior is influenced by the regular arrangement of atoms. The structure of the Brillouin zone makes it possible to predict properties such as electrical conductivity, band gaps, and optical responses.

Thus, the Brillouin zone plays a central role in explaining why some materials act as conductors, semiconductors, or insulators. Its study connects abstract mathematical ideas with practical applications in electronics, materials science, and modern technology.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main findings of a paper on quasi-2D spin-wave waveforms in longitudinally magnetized ferrimagnetic film stripes studied with time- and space-resolved Brillouin light scattering.
counterfactuals.output:
The paper’s main finding is that spin waves in longitudinally magnetized ferrimagnetic film stripes cannot generally be treated as simple one-dimensional waveguide modes. Using time- and space-resolved Brillouin light scattering, the authors directly imaged the evolution of pulsed spin-wave packets and showed that their waveforms are strongly quasi-two-dimensional.

Key conclusions include:

- **Quasi-2D propagation in a stripe geometry:**  
  Even though the magnetic film is patterned into a stripe, the excited spin waves spread across both the length and the width of the stripe. The observed intensity patterns show transverse structure rather than a uniform profile across the stripe.

- **Formation of characteristic wavefronts and interference patterns:**  
  The measured spin-wave packets develop complex spatial waveforms due to the superposition of different wave-vector components and lateral quantization across the stripe width. Reflections from the stripe edges and interference between transverse modes produce nontrivial intensity maxima and minima.

- **Strong role of dipolar spin-wave anisotropy:**  
  In the longitudinal magnetization configuration, the spin-wave dispersion is highly anisotropic. As a result, the group velocity direction does not necessarily coincide with the wave-vector direction, producing oblique energy flow and structured wavefronts.

- **Multiple transverse modes contribute:**  
  The experimental data indicate that the microwave antenna excites several width modes of the stripe. Their different phase velocities and group velocities lead to temporal and spatial beating, reshaping the propagating packet.

- **Time-resolved BLS reveals packet evolution directly:**  
  By mapping the spin-wave intensity as a function of position and delay time, the authors could follow how the initially excited waveform evolves, disperses, and interacts with the lateral boundaries.

- **Agreement with spin-wave theory/modeling:**  
  The observed waveforms are consistent with calculations based on the dipole-exchange spin-wave dispersion in a confined ferrimagnetic stripe. This confirms that the complex patterns arise from the intrinsic anisotropic dispersion and finite-width confinement rather than from experimental artifacts.

Overall, the study demonstrates that longitudinally magnetized ferrimagnetic film stripes support rich quasi-two-dimensional spin-wave dynamics. This has practical importance for magnonic waveguides and spin-wave logic devices, because signal propagation in such structures depends not only on propagation along the stripe but also on transverse mode structure, edge reflections, and anisotropic group-velocity effects.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract-style paragraph describing experiments on spin-wave propagation in confined ferrimagnetic film waveguides, including linear and nonlinear regimes and the role of edge pinning.
counterfactuals.output: We report experimental investigations of spin-wave propagation in confined ferrimagnetic film waveguides, focusing on the transition from the linear to nonlinear dynamical regimes and on the influence of lateral boundary conditions. Spin waves were excited and detected in micron- to millimeter-scale ferrimagnetic strips, where geometric confinement produces discrete transverse modes whose frequencies, group velocities, and attenuation depend sensitively on the effective pinning of the dynamic magnetization at the waveguide edges. In the low-power regime, the measured transmission spectra and propagation characteristics are well described by linear spin-wave theory when partial edge pinning is included, demonstrating that nonideal boundaries strongly modify the modal structure relative to unconfined films. At elevated excitation powers, nonlinear effects become prominent, including amplitude-dependent frequency shifts, mode coupling, spectral broadening, and changes in propagation length, reflecting the interplay between intrinsic magnetic nonlinearity and confinement-induced mode quantization. The results show that edge pinning not only determines the linear eigenmode spectrum but also governs the efficiency of nonlinear scattering channels by controlling modal overlap and dispersion. These findings highlight the importance of boundary conditions in designing ferrimagnetic magnonic waveguides and provide insight into the control of coherent spin-wave transport in both linear signal-processing and nonlinear magnonic applications.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a concise scientific summary about how lateral confinement affects dynamic magnetization and nonlinear spin-wave packet formation in ferrimagnetic film stripes.
counterfactuals.output:
Lateral confinement in ferrimagnetic film stripes strongly modifies spin-wave dynamics by imposing boundary conditions across the stripe width. This quantizes the transverse spin-wave modes, changes the internal demagnetizing field, and produces nonuniform dynamic magnetization profiles, often with enhanced amplitudes near the stripe edges or in specific width modes.

Compared with extended films, confined stripes have a discrete mode spectrum rather than a continuous one. The allowed modes depend on stripe width, thickness, bias-field orientation, and magnetic parameters such as saturation magnetization and exchange stiffness. This modifies the spin-wave dispersion, group velocity, damping behavior, and nonlinear frequency shift.

At high excitation powers, nonlinear effects become important. Lateral confinement can either suppress or promote nonlinear spin-wave packet formation depending on the stripe width. In narrow stripes, transverse spreading is restricted, favoring quasi-one-dimensional nonlinear wave packets such as dark or bright envelope solitons. In wider stripes, additional transverse modes become available, allowing self-focusing, mode coupling, and the formation of localized two-dimensional spin-wave packets, often described as spin-wave bullets.

Thus, lateral confinement controls both the spatial structure of the dynamic magnetization and the nonlinear evolution of propagating spin waves. By tailoring the stripe geometry, one can tune the transition between linear guided modes, one-dimensional nonlinear packets, and multidimensional localized spin-wave excitations in ferrimagnetic magnonic waveguides.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a journal-abstract-like conclusion for a study of quasi-two-dimensional spin-wave waveforms in magnetic stripe waveguides, mentioning effective dipolar pinning, transverse instability, side-wall interaction, and numerical simulations.
counterfactuals.output: In conclusion, we have investigated quasi-two-dimensional spin-wave waveforms in magnetic stripe waveguides, emphasizing the role of lateral confinement and boundary-induced effects in shaping their propagation characteristics. The results indicate that effective dipolar pinning at the stripe edges strongly modifies the transverse mode profiles and contributes to the formation of nonuniform wavefronts. As the spin waves propagate, transverse instability can emerge due to the coupling between longitudinal dynamics and laterally confined modes, leading to waveform distortion and mode redistribution. The interaction with the side walls is therefore a key mechanism governing both the spatial structure and stability of the propagating excitations. Numerical simulations support these findings, reproducing the observed evolution of quasi-two-dimensional waveforms and clarifying the interplay between dipolar pinning, lateral confinement, and side-wall-induced scattering. These results highlight the importance of edge effects in magnetic stripe waveguides and provide guidance for the design of magnonic devices based on controlled spin-wave propagation.
